newsitem.title: THAILAND: Tensions dampen Indo-China's New Year spirits.
newsitem.headline: Tensions dampen Indo-China's New Year spirits.

text.p: While revellers in Thailand indulged in frenzied water fights, political tensions overshadowed traditional New Year festivities in Burma and Cambodia this weekend, observers said.

In celebrations to mark the traditional New Year in most of mainland Southeast Asia, locals usually visit temples, pay respects to elders and throw water in Thailand, Laos, Burma, Cambodia and parts of southern China.
The festival is known in Thailand as Songkran and is traditionally celebrated for three days.
In the Thai capital of Bangkok, flat-bed trucks carrying barrels of water, buckets and watergun-toting youths toured the streets looking to drench residents.

In the budget traveller's ghetto of Khao Sarn, the roads, pavements and cars were awash with water and powder as international visitors and locals enjoyed the chance to let off steam and cool off at the height of the hot season.
"There have been some scores settled but it's all been done in really good humour," said Lucy Wallis, 30, from Bristol, England.
But in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh, recent and bloody score-settling dampened festivities, observers said.

Many residents stayed home after the deadly March 30 grenade attack on an opposition demonstration and because of tensions generated by deteriorating relations between the country's two main parties in the coalition government, observers said.
Part of the park opposite parliament where grenades killed 19 people and injured more than 100 remained cordoned off.
The park is usually crowded with shops and musicians and theatrical performers during long holidays.

Locals were seen heading to temples in the capital to pay their respects and seek blessings from saffron-robed monks but many Cambodians said they would be celebrating indoors because of security worries and strained ties between the royalist FUNCINPEC party and the Cambodian People's Party.

In Burma, the New Year festival, or Maha Thingyan, is a rare occasion the military government allows public gatherings but security was tighter than usual in the capital Rangoon after recent unrest among students, monks and an April 6 parcel bombing which killed the daughter of a top official, Lieutenant-General Tin Oo.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council, under its "Committee for Observing Discipline during Maha Thingyan", said it had posted officials around the city to ensure security.
A statement issued by the committee advised: "Stay clear of making disturbances and agitations that may lead to disintegration of national unity and a state of unrest."
Some government departments, ministries and private companies had begun dismantling stages built a few days ago for festival entertainment, observers said.
"The festival this year is not going to be very exciting. Concern for security has spoilt the thirst of the people for much fun," said one city resident.
